items.question: How large is a normal heart in the four-chamber plane?
options: Usually no larger than one third of the area of the chest
About two thirds of the area of the chest
About half the area of the chest
About one tenth of the area of the chest
items.explanation: A normal heart is usually no larger than one third of the chest area.

items.question: A thin dark rim, less than 2 mm thick, surrounds the heart at 22 weeks. How is this read?
options: Normal: a small amount of pericardial fluid is common
A pericardial effusion needing urgent referral
A sign of heart failure
An artefact that means the view must be repeated
items.explanation: Pericardial fluid of 2 mm or less at end-systole is common in the second and third trimesters and is normal; a small hypoechogenic rim should not be mistaken for an effusion.

items.question: Which landmark identifies the morphological right ventricle?
options: The moderator band near the apex
The smooth apex that forms the apex of the heart
The foramen ovale flap
The pulmonary veins
items.explanation: The moderator band near the apex identifies the right ventricle; the smooth left ventricle forms the apex of the heart.

items.question: In which chamber does the foramen ovale flap normally move?
options: The left atrium
The right atrium
The left ventricle
It does not move
items.explanation: The foramen ovale flap moves within the left atrium.

items.question: With the beam running along the septum, there seems to be a gap in the septum near the crux. What is the first thing to consider?
options: Acoustic drop-out; look again with the beam perpendicular to the septum
A definite atrioventricular septal defect
A definite large ventricular septal defect
A normal communication that needs no further look
items.explanation: With the beam parallel to the septum, drop-out can falsely suggest a defect near the crux. The septum is best seen with the beam perpendicular.

items.question: Which valve leaflet normally inserts closer to the apex?
options: The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve
The anterior leaflet of the mitral valve
Both insert at exactly the same level
The aortic valve
items.explanation: The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve inserts closer to the apex than the mitral valve; this is the normal offset.

items.question: At 20 weeks the left ventricle is clearly smaller than the right. Which of these is named as an important cause?
options: Coarctation of the aorta
A normal third-trimester variant
An echogenic intracardiac focus
Benign ectopic beats
items.explanation: Asymmetry in mid-gestation warrants further examination; important causes are coarctation, evolving hypoplastic left heart syndrome and anomalous pulmonary venous return.

items.question: What does the guideline say about a 1 to 2 mm ventricular septal defect?
options: It can be very difficult to confirm, and most are of limited clinical significance
It is always visible on grey-scale
It is always a sign of a chromosomal anomaly
It never closes before birth
items.explanation: Small septal defects (1 to 2 mm) can be very difficult to confirm; most are of limited clinical significance and may close spontaneously in utero.

items.question: Is colour Doppler required to show a pulmonary vein entering the left atrium at screening?
options: No: grey-scale where feasible; colour can help but is not mandatory
Yes: always
Yes: with pulsed-wave Doppler as well
Pulmonary veins are not part of the four-chamber criteria
items.explanation: At least one pulmonary vein should be seen entering the left atrium on B-mode when technically feasible; colour can help but is not mandatory.

items.question: The four-chamber view meets every criterion. Which lesion may still be present?
options: Transposition of the great arteries
A common atrioventricular valve
A heart filling two thirds of the chest
A single ventricle
items.explanation: Transposition and coarctation may not be evident in the four-chamber plane alone. The other three would break a four-chamber criterion.
